subproblem.title: Prescribed Frobenius in a prime-cyclotomic extension
subproblem.statement: Let Ω = AlgebraicClosure ℚ. Let M be a finite-dimensional intermediate field of Ω/ℚ, and let F be an intermediate field of M/ℚ. Let q be a natural prime and ζ ∈ M a primitive qth root of unity. Assume that adjoining ζ to F inside M gives all of M. For every F-automorphism h of M and every finite set B of natural numbers, there exist a natural prime ℓ outside B and a valuation subring W of M such that ℓ is a nonunit of W and h preserves W and acts on its residue field by x ↦ x^ℓ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (M : IntermediateField ℚ (AlgebraicClosure ℚ)) [FiniteDimensional ℚ M] (F : IntermediateField ℚ M) (q : ℕ) (ζ : M), q.Prime → IsPrimitiveRoot ζ q → IntermediateField.adjoin F ({ζ} : Set M) = ⊤ → ∀ (h : M ≃ₐ[F] M) (B : Finset ℕ), ∃ ℓ : ℕ, ℓ.Prime ∧ ℓ ∉ B ∧ ∃ W : ValuationSubring M, W.LiesOverPrime ℓ ∧ W.IsFrobeniusAt h ℓ
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Fix M,F,q,ζ,h,B as in the statement, and identify F with its image in Ω through M. We first establish the finite arithmetic and analytic facts used below. All fields considered are finite extensions of ℚ. They are separable: an irreducible characteristic-zero polynomial is relatively prime to its nonzero derivative. Successively extending embeddings across algebraic generators gives as many embeddings as the extension degree. Finite extensions are simple: for two generators a,b, distinct embeddings agree on a + rb for at most one rational r unless their b-images agree, in which case they never agree there. Avoid the finitely many exceptional values and induct on a generating family. Scaling gives an integral primitive element. For a finite Galois extension K/L and subgroup H, a primitive element has |H| distinct H-translates. Its orbit polynomial has coefficients in K^H, while all its translates are roots of its minimal polynomial over K^H. These two degree inequalities give [K:K^H] = |H|. Normality and separability give [K:L′] automorphisms over every intermediate field L′, so their fixed field is L′. Extension and restriction of embeddings then give the fixed-field correspondence and its normal-subgroup quotient assertion.
2. Every finite multiplicative subgroup of a field is cyclic. Let d be the least common multiple of its element orders. Suitable powers of elements supply each maximal prime-power order dividing d. The product of these elements has order d: for commuting elements of coprime orders, cancellation between powers would put an element in cyclic subgroups whose intersection is trivial. Every group element is a root of X^d−1, so the polynomial root bound gives at most d elements; the constructed element already has d distinct powers. The root bound follows by dividing by X−a and inducting on degree. This proves cyclicity of finite-field multiplicative groups and of the group of Nth roots of unity in Ω. In the latter case there are exactly N roots for N > 0, since X^N−1 splits and is separable.
3. For a degree-d number field K, its integer ring O_K is free of rank d over ℤ, Noetherian, integrally closed, and has fraction field K. Finitely many integral elements generate a finite module algebra because monic equations reduce their powers. Conversely, if multiplication by x preserves a nonzero finitely generated module in a field, a matrix of multiplication relations and the adjugate identity show that the monic determinant of xI minus that matrix vanishes. These arguments prove closure of integral elements and transitivity of integrality. Scale a rational basis to integral elements. The trace pairing is nondegenerate: on a primitive-element power basis its matrix is the transpose of the conjugate-evaluation matrix times that matrix, whose Vandermonde determinant is nonzero. Evaluation at conjugates also shows that trace is the sum of conjugates. Traces of integral elements are rational integers, since a reduced rational fraction satisfying a monic integer equation has denominator one. Thus O_K lies between the scaled-basis lattice and its trace-dual lattice. A subgroup of ℤ^d is finite free: project to one coordinate, lift a generator of its cyclic image, split off that summand, and induct on the kernel. The lattice bounds give rank d. Ideals are finitely generated as additive groups, hence as ideals. Transitivity proves integral closedness and denominator clearing proves the fraction-field assertion.
4. Every nonzero prime 𝔭 of O_K is maximal with finite residue field, and its localization is a discrete valuation ring. For nonzero a ∈ 𝔭, the nonzero constant term of its monic integral minimal polynomial belongs to 𝔭, so 𝔭 contains a rational prime. The quotient is consequently a finite domain and hence a field. The localization A is one-dimensional, Noetherian, local, and integrally closed. Integral closedness localizes: multiplying a root of a monic equation by a common denominator outside 𝔭 makes it integral over O_K. To obtain a uniformizer, write 𝔪 for the nonzero maximal ideal and choose 0 ≠ a ∈ 𝔪. The only prime containing (a) is 𝔪, so √(a) = 𝔪; the radical criterion follows by localizing at powers of an element outside the radical and contracting a maximal ideal. Finite generation gives a least n ≥ 1 with 𝔪^n ⊆ (a). If n = 1, then 𝔪 = (a). Otherwise choose b ∈ 𝔪^(n−1) outside (a) and put x = b/a. Then x𝔪 ⊆ A but x ∉ A. If x𝔪 ⊆ 𝔪, the determinant argument on the finite nonzero module 𝔪 makes x integral, a contradiction. Hence xy is a unit for some y ∈ 𝔪. For z ∈ 𝔪, z/y = (xz)/(xy) lies in A, so 𝔪 = (y). A nonzero element cannot belong to every (y^j), because the ascending principal ideals generated by its successive quotients would stabilize and force y to be a unit. Every nonzero element is therefore a largest power of y times a unit. Differences of exponents give the discrete valuation on K.
5. Nonzero fractional ideals of O_K factor uniquely into prime ideals with integer exponents. For an integral ideal I, use the minimum valuation of its finite generators at each prime. Only finitely many minima are positive: for 0 ≠ a ∈ I, multiplication by a on an integral basis has nonzero integer determinant, so O_K/(a) is finite and has finitely many primes. The product of the prescribed prime powers has the same localization as I everywhere. Localizations detect membership: if x ∉ J, a maximal ideal containing the proper ideal {r : rx ∈ J} detects the failure after localization. Thus they detect equality. The inverse I⁻¹ = {x ∈ K : xI ⊆ O_K} is finitely generated over ℤ, since multiplication by a nonzero element of I embeds it into O_K. Clearing denominators on finite generators shows that inversion commutes with localization. Hence II⁻¹ is locally, and therefore globally, the unit ideal. Denominator clearing extends factorization to fractional ideals; valuations give uniqueness.
6. Define N(I) = |O_K/I| for nonzero integral ideals. Norms multiply, and N((a)) = |N_{K/ℚ}(a)|. Distinct prime powers are comaximal, as follows by expanding a sufficiently high power of a+b = 1 with a,b in the distinct primes. Chinese remaindering separates their quotients. At a single prime, localization does not change successive prime-power quotients, and a uniformizer identifies each with a one-dimensional residue-field space. Thus N(𝔭^e) = N(𝔭)^e. For principal ideals, integer row and column reductions identify lattice index with the absolute determinant of multiplication by a. Denominators extend these formulas to fractional ideals. Only finitely many integral ideals have bounded norm: one of norm n contains nO_K and corresponds to a subgroup of the finite additive group O_K/nO_K.
7. At most [K:ℚ] primes of K lie above a rational prime ℓ. Chinese remaindering gives a quotient of O_K/ℓO_K whose dimension is the sum of their positive residue degrees. Every nonzero prime of a number field L has a prime above it in a finite extension K. Localize the integral extension of integer rings away from the lower prime and take a maximal ideal upstairs. Its contraction is maximal: if a field is integral over a domain, a monic equation for the inverse of a nonzero element expresses that inverse in the domain. The local base ring has only the specified maximal ideal.
8. In a finite Galois extension K/L with group J, J acts transitively on primes above a fixed lower prime. Otherwise Chinese remaindering supplies an integral element a with residue zero on one orbit and one on another. The product of all J-translates of a lies in O_L but has residues zero and one above the same lower prime, a contradiction.
9. The decomposition group J_𝔓 surjects onto the automorphism group of the residue extension. Suppose b̄ is fixed by the image. Choose integral a with residue b̄ at 𝔓 and zero at the other primes over the lower prime. The polynomial ∏_{u∈J}(T−u(a)) lies in O_L[T] and reduces at 𝔓 to T^(|J|−|J_𝔓|)(T−b̄)^|J_𝔓|. Write |J_𝔓| = r^v u with r the residue characteristic and r not dividing u. The coefficient of degree |J|−r^v is −u b̄^(r^v). Therefore b̄^(r^v) belongs to the lower residue field. The r^v-power map is bijective there and injective upstairs, so b̄ belongs to the lower field. If the residue sizes are Q and Q^f, the Q-power automorphism has order f: its fth power is the identity and the root bound excludes any smaller positive power. There are at most f automorphisms, since a generator of the upper multiplicative group generates the field. Thus the residue Galois group is cyclic of order f. A proper subgroup is generated by the dth power of Frobenius for a divisor d > 1 of f. Its fixed field contains all Q^d distinct roots of X^(Q^d)−X; these lie upstairs because this polynomial divides X^(Q^f)−X. This contradicts the fixed-element conclusion. Surjectivity follows.
10. For any finite extension K/L and lower prime 𝔭, [K:L] = Σ_{𝔓|𝔭} e_𝔓 f_𝔓. Localizing O_K over (O_L)_𝔭 gives a finite torsion-free module of rank [K:L] over a discrete valuation ring. Such a module is free: project its fraction vector space to a nonzero coordinate, note that the finite image is a principal fractional ideal, lift its generator, split off that summand, and induct. Reduction modulo 𝔭, prime-power filtrations, and Chinese remaindering give the formula. In the Galois case e and f are constant by transitivity, so orbit–stabilizer gives |J_𝔓| = ef. Step 9 gives inertia order e. At an unramified prime there is therefore a unique decomposition-group element inducing arithmetic residue Frobenius, and it has order f. Conjugation conjugates these elements, and restriction to Galois subextensions preserves them.
11. For every number field K the ideal series ζ_K(s) = Σ_{I≠0} N(I)^−s converges absolutely for Re(s) > 1 and equals its Euler product. Step 7 bounds the prime-ideal sum by [K:ℚ]Σ_ℓ ℓ^−Re(s), bounded by the convergent integer series. After removing finitely many factors, −log(1−x) ≤ 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1/2 proves product convergence. Expanding finite products and using unique factorization proves the series identity. The same estimates are uniform on compact subsets of this half-plane.
12. For a number field L of degree d = r₁+2r₂, let W_∞ = ℝ^r₁ × ℂ^r₂. Factoring a primitive polynomial over ℝ and applying polynomial Chinese remaindering identifies L⊗ℚℝ with W_∞. The complex splitting input is the fundamental theorem of algebra, specifically Complex.exists_root in the pinned mathlib file Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Polynomial/Basic.lean, lines 35–53, revision db584cd6d46c92f209a44c0f1c829460d327499d. An integral basis identifies O_L with a full lattice of covolume Δ_L > 0. A fractional ideal 𝔞 has covolume Δ_L N(𝔞), by the index and determinant formulas. Integrating the number of translates of a bounded measurable set over a lattice fundamental parallelepiped shows that volume greater than the covolume forces two distinct points to differ by a lattice vector. Applied to half a symmetric convex body, this gives a nonzero lattice point whenever its volume exceeds 2^d times the covolume.
13. The ordinary ideal class group of L is finite. Apply step 12 to an integral ideal 𝔞 and a product of intervals and disks of radii cN(𝔞)^(1/d), with c sufficiently large and fixed. It supplies 0 ≠ a ∈ 𝔞 with |N_{L/ℚ}(a)| ≤ c^d N(𝔞). The norm is the product of absolute real coordinates and squared complex moduli, by diagonalizing multiplication through the embeddings. The integral ideal (a)𝔞⁻¹ represents the inverse class and has bounded norm. Step 6 gives finitely many possibilities. Clearing denominators gives integral representatives of all fractional ideal classes.
14. Unit logarithms form a full lattice. Give real places weight e_v = 1 and complex places weight e_v = 2, and set H₀ = {x : Σ_v e_v x_v = 0}. For a unit u, λ(u) = (log|u|_v) belongs to H₀ since its absolute norm is one. Bounded logarithms bound all embeddings, so lattice discreteness gives only finitely many such units. Hence the logarithmic image Λ is discrete and its kernel is finite; this kernel is precisely the roots of unity, because a finite multiplicative group consists of elements of finite order. For x ∈ H₀, apply step 12 with radii c exp(x_v). Their weighted product is fixed. The resulting nonzero integral a has all differences log|a|_v−x_v bounded above. Their weighted sum is log|N(a)| ≥ 0, so each difference is also bounded below. The norm |N(a)| is bounded, leaving only finitely many ideals (a). Choose generators b_j for these ideals. Then a/b_j is a unit with logarithm within a fixed distance of x. Thus Λ spans H₀. Choose a real basis from Λ and let Λ₀ be its integer span. A bounded fundamental parallelepiped contains representatives for Λ/Λ₀, so this quotient is finite. If its order is k, then kΛ ⊆ Λ₀; the subgroup argument for ℤ^r gives a lattice basis for Λ. The argument includes dimension zero.
15. A modulus 𝔣 consists of a nonzero integral ideal 𝔣₀ and specified real places. Its ray class group is the group of fractional ideals supported away from 𝔣₀ modulo principal ideals generated by elements congruent to one at the finite modulus and positive at the specified real places. It is finite. Forgetting the ray conditions maps it to the finite ordinary class group. In its kernel, generators have valuation zero at modulus primes; their residues and signs lie in the finite group (O_L/𝔣₀)ˣ × {±1}^{𝔣∞}. Denominators prime to the modulus exist by Chinese remaindering, and cross-multiplication makes the residue independent of the denominator. Thus the kernel is a quotient of a finite group. Every ray class has an integral representative prime to 𝔣₀: its denominator ideal is coprime to 𝔣₀, so choose in it an element congruent to one modulo 𝔣₀. Adding a sufficiently large positive multiple of a positive rational integer in both that ideal and 𝔣₀ preserves these conditions and ensures the required signs.
16. Fix an integral representative 𝔞 of a ray class C, prime to 𝔣₀. The nonzero integral ideals in C prime to 𝔣₀ are exactly a𝔞 with nonzero a ∈ 1+𝔣₀𝔞⁻¹ satisfying the prescribed signs. At modulus primes this is the ray congruence because 𝔞 is locally the unit ideal. Elsewhere it is equivalent to a ∈ 𝔞⁻¹ because 𝔣₀ is locally the unit ideal and 1 ∈ 𝔞⁻¹. Localization detects the global assertion. Two parameters give the same ideal exactly when their quotient is a ray unit. The ray units U_𝔣 have finite index in O_Lˣ by the finite residue-and-sign map. Their logarithmic image Λ_𝔣 is a full lattice in H₀, with finite logarithmic kernel of order w_𝔣 ≥ 1.
17. Choose a half-open fundamental parallelepiped P for Λ_𝔣. For z ∈ W_∞ with nonzero coordinates, put r = |N(z)|^(1/d) and b_v = log|z_v|−log r. Let ℛ be the region defined by 0 < r ≤ 1, b ∈ P, the prescribed positive real signs, all choices of other real signs, and all complex arguments. It is bounded and has positive volume: the radial, logarithmic, and angular parameters give local coordinates with nonsingular derivatives in the interior. Its boundary is contained in finitely many Lipschitz images of bounded (d−1)-dimensional boxes, together with the origin. Indeed, the formulas ±r exp(b_v) and r exp(b_v+iθ_v) have bounded derivatives on closed parameter boxes, and their faces cover the boundary away from the origin. Each admissible ray-unit orbit has exactly w_𝔣 representatives with logarithmic component in P. There is a unique logarithmic lattice translate into P, and the logarithmic kernel acts freely on nonzero elements, preserving r and the required signs.
18. For a full lattice Λ′ and any translate z₀+Λ′, the number of points in tℛ, for t ≥ 1, is vol(ℛ)t^d/covol(Λ′) + O(t^(d−1)). Tile the space by bounded fundamental cells anchored at translated lattice points. Cells whose closures avoid the boundary contribute equally to the point count and normalized volume. Subdivide each boundary parameter box into O(t^(d−1)) boxes of side at most 1/t. After dilation, every image has bounded diameter and meets a uniformly bounded number of cells, by positive minimum lattice separation and bounded cell diameter. Only O(t^(d−1)) cells contribute error. The origin and half-open faces satisfy the same bound; in dimension one it is O(1).
19. Apply step 18 to 1+𝔣₀𝔞⁻¹ and divide by w_𝔣. The bound N(a𝔞) ≤ X corresponds to t = (X/N(𝔞))^(1/d). Since covol(𝔣₀𝔞⁻¹) = Δ_L N(𝔣₀)/N(𝔞), the number A_C(X) of these ideals is κ_𝔣 X + O(X^(1−1/d)), where κ_𝔣 = vol(ℛ)/(w_𝔣 Δ_L N(𝔣₀)) > 0 is independent of C. Enlarging the error constant covers bounded X, t < 1, and exclusion of the zero parameter.
20. Summation by parts gives ζ_C(s) = s∫₁∞ A_C(t)t^(−s−1)dt for Re(s) > 1. The main term is κ_𝔣 s/(s−1). The error integral is holomorphic for Re(s) > 1−1/d: on compact subsets all differentiated integrands are bounded by integrable multiples of t^(−1−ε)(1+log t)^j. Uniform convergence of truncated integrals and their derivatives justifies differentiation. Thus ζ_C(s) = κ_𝔣/(s−1) plus a function holomorphic near one. Taking the trivial modulus and summing over the ordinary ideal classes proves that ζ_L has a positive simple-pole limit along real s decreasing to one. No prime distribution or reciprocity has been used.
21. Return to the fixed extension M = F(ζ). It is the splitting field of X^q−1 over F, hence finite Galois. Its group J embeds in (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ through the exponent action on ζ, so is cyclic by step 2. Away from q, reduction on qth roots of unity is injective. The roots and their inverses are integral, hence units in the upper valuation ring. If a nonidentity qth root ξ reduced to one, cancellation of ξ−1 in ξ^q−1 followed by reduction of the geometric sum would give q = 0 in the residue field, a contradiction. Thus inertia fixes ζ and is trivial away from q. Arithmetic Frobenius at a prime 𝔭 of F acts on ζ with exponent N(𝔭), because its residue action does and reduction on these roots is injective.
22. Let T consist of the primes of F above q and above the rational primes belonging to B. It is finite by step 7. The free abelian group of fractional ideals supported outside T has a homomorphism Φ_T to J sending a prime to its Frobenius. The element is independent of the upper prime because J is abelian. Under J → (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ, Φ_T is the positive rational ideal norm reduced modulo q. Set 𝔣₀ = qO_F times the product of the primes in T, and include all real places in the modulus. For a satisfying the ray conditions, its denominator ideal I = {x ∈ O_F : xa ∈ O_F} has no factors above q. Thus b = N(I) is prime to q, bO_F ⊆ I, and ba is integral. At primes above q, a−1 lies locally in qO_F, so ba−b does also. At other primes q is a unit and ba−b is integral. Localization yields ba−b ∈ qO_F globally. Multiplication by ba on an integral basis is therefore congruent to b times the identity modulo q. Taking determinants and dividing by b^[F:ℚ] gives N_{F/ℚ}(a) ≡ 1 modulo q. This norm is positive, since all real factors are positive and nonreal factors occur in conjugate pairs. Thus the positive ideal norm N((a)) has residue one. Injectivity of the exponent action shows Φ_T((a)) = 1, so Φ_T descends to a homomorphism Art from the ray class group to J. The support of this modulus is exactly T.
23. Art is surjective. Let H be its image and F′ = M^H. Since J is abelian, F′/F is Galois. Every prime outside T is unramified and has trivial Frobenius in F′, so splits into d′ = [F′:F] primes of residue degree one. Euler products give ζ_{F′}, with factors above T removed, equal to the d′th power of ζ_F with its T-factors removed. Step 20 gives positive simple-pole asymptotics for both zeta functions, and the removed finite factors have positive nonzero limits. If d′ > 1, multiplication by (s−1)^d′ makes the left side tend to zero and the right side tend to a positive number. Hence d′ = 1 and H = J.
24. For each complex character ψ of J define L_T(s,ψ) = ∏_{𝔭∉T}(1−ψ(Frob_𝔭)N(𝔭)^−s)⁻¹ on Re(s) > 1. Character values have modulus one, so step 11 gives absolute, locally uniform convergence, including the Euler logarithm. If ψ is nontrivial, its pullback θ through Art is nontrivial by surjectivity. Its sum over the ray class group is zero: translating by a class on which θ differs from one preserves the sum and multiplies it by a scalar different from one. Consequently the equal residues in step 20 cancel in Σ_C θ(C)ζ_C(s). Ideal factorization and absolute convergence identify this expression with L_T(s,ψ), since the modulus has support exactly T. Every nontrivial L_T(s,ψ) is therefore holomorphic near one.
25. Write m = |J|. At a prime outside T whose Frobenius has order f, the m characters take each fth root of unity exactly m/f times. Therefore ∏_ψ(1−ψ(Frob_𝔭)X) = (1−X^f)^(m/f). Step 10 gives m/f upper primes, each of norm N(𝔭)^f. Multiplying the local identities proves that ζ_M with factors above T removed equals ∏_ψ L_T(s,ψ). The trivial-character factor is ζ_F with T-factors removed. Their quotient has a positive nonzero limit at one by step 20. All the other factors have finite limits by step 24, so none vanishes at one. If m = 1 there are no nontrivial factors.
26. For real s decreasing to one, Σ_{𝔭∉T} ψ(Frob_𝔭)N(𝔭)^−s = δ_{ψ,1} log(1/(s−1)) + O(1). Write Eψ(s) = Σ_{𝔭∉T} Σ_{k≥1} ψ(Frob_𝔭)^k/(kN(𝔭)^(ks)) for the Euler logarithm. Absolute, locally uniform convergence gives exp(Eψ(s)) = L_T(s,ψ) and continuity for s > 1. The terms with k ≥ 2 have total absolute value at most 2Σ_𝔭 N(𝔭)^−2, uniformly for s > 1, by the geometric-series bound and N(𝔭) ≥ 2. This bound is finite by step 7. For the trivial character Eψ(s) is the real logarithm of the positive Euler product; the positive simple-pole asymptotic gives log(1/(s−1)) + O(1). For a nontrivial character put A = L_T(1,ψ), which is nonzero by step 25. Choose c ∈ ℂ with exp(c) = A, for example c = Complex.log A by Complex.exp_log in the pinned Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Complex/Log.lean. Continuity at one lets us choose ε > 0 so that |L_T(s,ψ)/A−1| < 1/2 whenever |s−1| < ε. On |z−1| < 1 define Log(z) = Σ_{n≥1} (−1)^(n+1)(z−1)^n/n. On |z−1| ≤ 1/2 this series converges uniformly and has absolute value at most Σ_{n≥1} 2^−n/n = log 2. Termwise differentiation gives Log′(z) = 1/z; therefore exp(Log(z))/z has derivative zero and equals one at z = 1, proving exp(Log(z)) = z throughout this disk. Define Hψ(s) = c + Log(L_T(s,ψ)/A). It is continuous and bounded near one, and exp(Hψ(s)) = exp(c)L_T(s,ψ)/A = L_T(s,ψ). Consequently Eψ(s)−Hψ(s) is continuous on the connected real interval 1 < s < 1+ε and belongs to 2πiℤ, since its exponential is one. The exponential-kernel identity is Complex.exp_eq_one_iff in the same pinned file. A continuous map from an interval to this discrete set is constant. Hence Eψ(s) is bounded on that interval. Removing its uniformly bounded k ≥ 2 tail proves the claimed estimate for every character.
27. For a ∈ J, cyclic character orthogonality gives Σ_{𝔭∉T,Frob_𝔭=a} N(𝔭)^−s = m⁻¹ log(1/(s−1)) + O(1). Indeed, m⁻¹Σ_ψ conjugate(ψ(a))ψ(b) is the indicator of a = b by the finite geometric-sum identity. Multiply the estimates in step 26 by these coefficients and sum; absolute convergence permits rearrangement. Primes of rational residue degree at least two have norm at least ℓ², with at most [F:ℚ] primes above each ℓ. Their total contribution remains bounded as s decreases to one. Removing them leaves a divergent sum, so there are infinitely many rational-residue-degree-one primes of F outside T with Frobenius a.
28. Apply step 27 to a = h. Choose such a prime 𝔭 and an upper prime 𝔓 of M, and let ℓ be the rational prime below 𝔭. Its residue degree one gives N(𝔭) = ℓ. Since 𝔭 lies outside T, ℓ ∉ B. Let W = (O_M)_𝔓, embedded in M. Step 4 makes this a valuation subring, and ℓ belongs to its maximal ideal, so W.LiesOverPrime ℓ. The relative Frobenius h preserves 𝔓 and hence W. The residue field of W is O_M/𝔓, and its actual decomposition-subgroup action is x ↦ x^N(𝔭) = x^ℓ. The identity extends to localized fractions by applying it to numerator and denominator. Thus W.IsFrobeniusAt h ℓ, proving every part of the stated conclusion.
proof_key_steps: Establish finite Galois theory, integer-ring ideal arithmetic, and the decomposition/inertia degree formulas.
Prove absolute convergence and the ideal Euler product for number-field zeta functions.
Use lattice geometry to prove finite class groups and the full unit-logarithm lattice.
Count ideals in each ray class with a common positive leading coefficient and a power-saving error.
Deduce equal simple-pole residues for ray-class partial zeta functions.
Construct the cyclotomic Artin map explicitly from ideal norms modulo q.
Prove Artin-map surjectivity by comparing zeta pole orders in its fixed field.
Use ray-class characters and the zeta product identity to prove nonvanishing of nontrivial character L-functions at one.
Add a logarithm c of L_T(1,ψ) to the bounded power-series logarithm of L_T(s,ψ)/L_T(1,ψ); compare it with the Euler logarithm on a connected interval, then apply character orthogonality.
Remove higher rational residue degrees and construct the required localization valuation with the actual prime-power residue action.

audit.reason: The exact type matches the prose, including the F-algebra structure, primitive-root and adjoining hypotheses, and actual F-linear residue action. The 28-step proof supplies the arithmetic, ray-class counting, equal residues, explicit Artin map, surjectivity and L-function nonvanishing arguments without invoking the parent or a distribution theorem. Step 26 correctly includes c with exp(c)=L_T(1,ψ), making the logarithm difference continuous and valued in 2πiℤ. Orthogonality and the bounded higher-degree contribution yield the required prime; localization proves every valuation conjunct. The proof is complete enough for formalization without another prose-generation pass.
